0.project: Compile and run C on your Mac and in an ARM64 Linux VM.
0.core: A working toolchain and a repeatable build script. Performance counters can wait.
checks: Compile a warning-clean hello program on the Mac
Compile and run the same program in the Linux VM
Explain working directory, stdout, stderr and exit status
0.rationale: Setup and the tool loop are already substantially complete per LEARNING.md. Do not repeat talks or reinstall tools. Only close the Linux-guest gap if it remains open; otherwise move on.

units.title: Verify the ARM64 Linux guest only if missing
units.outcome: Confirm a Linux environment with uname, compiler and basic tool availability, then record what it is and is not suitable for.

read.title: OrbStack Linux machines
read.scope: Machine creation and entering a Linux machine; skip if an ARM64 guest already works.
read.why: The roadmap needs Linux APIs, not a second host setup or x86 performance environment.
read.access: Public documentation; software licensing may differ

units.build: If there is no guest, create an Ubuntu ARM64 guest and verify uname -m, clang or gcc, and a trivial compiled program. Otherwise skip this unit.
units.stop: Stop when the existing Mac build loop remains clean and a Linux guest can compile and run a hello program. Do not revisit the mindset talks or performance counters here.

lookups.title: Missing Semester: The Shell
lookups.scope: Only the sections needed to resolve a concrete gap in paths, pipes, redirection, or shell execution.
lookups.why: A just-in-time lookup; the learner already has a build loop.

lookups.title: Dive Into Systems: GDB
lookups.scope: Section 3.1: break, step, locals, memory and backtrace only if the Linux debugger is still unfamiliar. Keep LLDB for the native Mac.
lookups.why: Linux tool orientation repairs a concrete gap; do not repeat the C course.

excluded.title: Clean Code, Horrible Performance and Data-Oriented Design talks
excluded.reason: Viewpoints, not toolchain prerequisites. They remain in the original archive; no talk queue blocks starting the C project.

excluded.title: Repeat the full machine installation checklist
excluded.reason: LEARNING.md records a working local clang loop; repeat setup only to fix a concrete missing capability.

1.project: Build the Hack CPU in HDL and an assembler.
1.core: Nand2Tetris projects 1–6 pass their supplied tests. A Hack emulator is stretch.
1.rationale: Nand2Tetris Part I is the only CPU build track. Each specification and its tests define a small deliverable; physical hardware videos are optional context, not a second computer to build.

units.title: Gates and truth tables
units.outcome: Build combinational gates from NAND and trace a mux.

read.title: Nand2Tetris: Boolean Logic
read.scope: Project 1 specification and supplied chip tests.
read.why: One concrete interface per chip, with tests rather than another logic course.

units.build: Implement the required gates and muxes in HDL. Trace two input cases by hand.
units.stop: All project 1 test scripts pass; you can explain why outputs have no clocked state.

units.title: Adders and the ALU
units.outcome: Turn gates into arithmetic and a configurable ALU.

read.title: Nand2Tetris: Boolean Arithmetic
read.scope: Project 2: half adder, full adder, incrementer and ALU.
read.why: Continues the same build instead of introducing another CPU design.

visual.title: Ben Eater: arithmetic logic unit
visual.scope: Only the ALU demonstration videos on this page. No kit purchase or breadboard build.
visual.why: Physical wiring helps you see signals that the HDL simulator abstracts.

units.build: Build the chips and trace one add, one AND and one zero/negative result.
units.stop: The official ALU tests pass and you can derive each control bit’s effect.

units.title: Clocked state and machine instructions
units.outcome: Distinguish combinational output from stored state.

read.title: Nand2Tetris: Sequential Logic
read.scope: Project 3: registers, RAM and program counter. Use the supplied D flip-flop primitive.
read.why: This is the actual boundary between logic and a computer that remembers.

units.build: Complete project 3. Then do project 4’s small machine-language exercises from the same Part I navigation before CPU assembly.
units.stop: Stateful chips pass tests and you can predict their output before and after a clock edge.

units.title: CPU and computer
units.outcome: Trace one instruction through fetch, ALU, register write and next PC.

read.title: Nand2Tetris: Computer Architecture
read.scope: Project 5 specification, CPU and computer tests. Review the linked project 4 instruction contract only if needed.
read.why: Reuses the chips you built; no separate CPU curriculum.

units.build: Wire the CPU and computer. Run supplied programs and trace one conditional jump.
units.stop: Project 5 tests pass and you can explain where one instruction’s bits affect the hardware.

units.title: Assembler and byte-identical output
units.outcome: Translate symbols and mnemonics into the machine’s 16-bit words.

read.title: Nand2Tetris: Assembler
read.scope: Project 6 only. Two-pass symbol resolution and the official comparison programs.
read.why: This is the reverse encoding problem used again in phase 3.

units.build: Write the assembler in C or Python. Compare Pong output byte-for-byte with the supplied assembler.
units.stop: Pong.hack matches. Stop Part I here; Part II and a second CPU build are not prerequisites.

lookups.title: Nand2Tetris: Machine Language
lookups.scope: Use the Hack instruction and memory-map contract while doing projects 4–6.
lookups.why: The one machine-language reference for this CPU.

excluded.title: Nand2Tetris Part II
excluded.reason: Jack compiler/OS overlaps later compiler study; phase 1 is explicitly Part I projects 1-6.

excluded.title: Build Ben Eater's separate breadboard CPU
excluded.reason: Video is optional visual context; a second full CPU build duplicates the Nand2Tetris outcome.

2.project: An arena-based string/container library and a tested JSON parser.
2.core: Correct ownership, checked allocation arithmetic, alignment and JSON accept/reject results. Do not grow a general-purpose library.
2.rationale: The phase is an applied C/library project, not a survey of every C resource. Use Modern C and CS:APP where they specify language and representation; add only the arena lifetime article and RFC where they directly support the build.

units.title: C object model, bits, and undefined behavior
units.outcome: Explain valid object bounds/lifetimes, integer and floating representations, and test small C code with sanitizers.

read.title: Modern C: object and pointer rules
read.scope: Modern C level 2 sections on pointers, object bounds, structs, alignment and lifetime. Review a level 0/1 rule only if a test exposes a gap. Keep the C11 baseline; level 3 waits for concurrency.
read.why: Primary language reference without taking a second introductory programming course.
read.access: Free author-hosted book; site fetch was unavailable during research, so confirm current PDF navigation

units.build: Inspect a struct's size, alignment and bytes in LLDB. Test object bounds and lifetime failures with address/undefined-behavior sanitizers where supported. Representation exercises are in the next step.
units.stop: Stop once bounds, lifetime, padding, integer representation, and sanitizer limits are understood for code actually used; do not read level 3 threads/atomics.

units.title: Data Lab and representation practice
units.outcome: Use bit-level reasoning to explain two's complement and IEEE-754 representations rather than rely on casts or intuition.

read.title: CS:APP: Data Lab
read.scope: Read the Data Lab handout and implement the integer/float puzzles. If you own CS:APP, chapter 2 is a reference for a stuck representation question, not another required reading queue.
read.why: This bounded exercise connects C integer rules to actual machine representations and supports phase 4 later.
read.access: Book access varies; Data Lab materials publicly listed

units.build: Complete the Data Lab exercises appropriate to chapter 2 and dump float/integer bits using memcpy-safe representation inspection.
units.stop: Stop when each representation exercise has a passing test and explanation. Do not start CS:APP chapters 3+ here.

units.title: Arena allocation, strings, and ownership
units.outcome: Implement an arena with checked size/alignment, length-carrying string views, and a clear owner/expiry model.

read.title: Untangling Lifetimes: The Arena Allocator
read.scope: The article's arena lifetime and permanent/scratch ownership discussion; read alongside the actual arena implementation, not as a full allocator survey.
read.why: It gives a visual/operational lifetime model that complements the precise C language rules.

visual.title: Handmade Hero day 034: Tile Map Memory
visual.scope: Only 49:50–54:58: memory_index, InitializeArena and PushStruct. Compare with your aligned arena; skip the preceding tile-map build and Win32 calls.
visual.why: A short visible allocation walkthrough complements the arena-lifetime text.

units.build: Build arena, Str, growable array and the parser’s open-addressed hash map. Test zero count, exact fit, exhaustion, alignment, overflow and container boundaries. Document views invalidated by reset or array growth. The formatter is the next step.
units.stop: Stop when all allocation invariants have tests and no returned view outlives its backing storage. No malloc-per-object redesign.

units.title: Bounded formatting and output
units.outcome: Append formatted bytes into a buffer with explicit capacity and error handling.

read.title: Wellons: Buffered, formatted output
read.scope: The append-buffer/error model and integer formatting only. Build the formatter your library and serializer need, not a full printf clone.
read.why: This covers a distinct required library mechanism instead of adding another general C course.

units.build: Implement bounded append and integer formatting; test empty/full/exact-fit buffers, negative values and sticky failure. Handle partial file writes at the output boundary.
units.stop: The formatter passes its focused driver, reports insufficient capacity and never loses a partial-write suffix.

units.title: JSON parser and conformance tests
units.outcome: Build a bounded recursive-descent JSON parser with explicit error offsets and documented number/string behavior.

read.title: RFC 8259 sections 2-7
read.scope: Sections 2-7 only: JSON grammar, values, strings, numbers, objects and arrays.
read.why: The RFC is the syntax contract for the parser, not another programming curriculum.

units.build: Build both parser and serializer on your library. Add arrays, objects, strings/escapes and numbers incrementally. Test JSONTestSuite y_ accept and n_ reject cases, depth/bounds/truncation, trailing junk and round trips. Use an independent parser or known fixtures too: a round trip alone can hide shared bugs.
units.stop: JSONTestSuite accept/reject cases and serializer fixtures pass, and implementation-dependent outcomes are documented. Do not grow a general-purpose framework beyond these callers.

lookups.title: JSONTestSuite
lookups.scope: Run y_ cases as accepted and n_ cases as rejected; document i_ outcomes.
lookups.why: External test corpus supplements hand-written tests without duplicating tutorial coverage.

excluded.title: Advanced C Programming course
excluded.reason: Optional and broad; it duplicates the concrete Modern C, arena, and parser work. Consult a specific lesson only if a gap appears.

excluded.title: Modern C level 3 and concurrency topics
excluded.reason: The roadmap defers threads and atomics to phase 6.

3.project: ARM64 and x86-64 programs, then an 8086 decoder and simulator.
3.core: Correct ABI boundaries and round-trip decoding first. Benchmark only on the matching native ISA.
3.rationale: Learn calling conventions and emitted code from short exercises, then do one real decoder/simulator track. Preserve the phase's ARM64 and x86 contrast without adding more introductory assembly courses.

units.title: ARM64 function and ABI on the Mac
units.outcome: Write and call small assembly functions from C, preserving registers and explaining argument/return registers and stack alignment.

read.title: HelloSilicon examples
read.scope: Examples matching Stephen Smith chapters 1-7: registers, arithmetic, branches, memory, calls/stack, and OS calls. Select one example per operation; do not read the whole book independently of the repo.
read.why: The repository adapts examples to Apple Silicon and calls out macOS differences.
read.access: Free source repository; referenced book may require purchase

units.build: Start with an ARM64 add called from C, then a nested call. Continue the roadmap’s small strlen, memcpy, array sum, fib and hello exercises; step with LLDB and verify saved registers and 16-byte stack alignment.
units.stop: The small programs and nested call work through the C ABI, and the register/stack protocol is explainable. Do not add a large assembly program.

units.title: Repeat the ABI exercise on x86-64 Linux
units.outcome: Compare the two ISAs' argument registers, return address handling, saved registers, and stack frames.

read.title: Dive Into Systems: 64-bit x86 Assembly
read.scope: Read 7.2 common instructions and the function/calling-convention sections for the existing add/nested-call exercise. Consult arrays/structs only when annotating that function; do not read all of chapter 7.
read.why: A free, bounded online text with independently addressable x86-64 topics. It replaces the older broad UNLV PDF as the reading reference while retaining the existing small add/nested-call build.

units.build: Repeat the small ARM64 exercises and nested call in an explicitly x86-64 Linux environment. Annotate argument/return registers and stack behavior beside the ARM versions.
units.stop: The same small programs and nested call run on both targets and the ABI contrast is clear. An ARM64 VM is not x86-64 execution.

units.title: Compiler output and linking
units.outcome: Read one C function at -O0/-O2, identify common transformations, and explain objects, symbols, and relocations.

read.title: CS:APP chapter 7: Linking
read.scope: Chapter 7 only: object files, symbols, relocations and linking. Reuse the preceding Dive Into Systems instruction/ABI explanation when inspecting compiler output; do not repeat CS:APP chapter 3. The lab handouts follow the decoder step.
read.why: Linking adds a distinct binary-toolchain mechanism; the assembly explanation was already assigned in the previous step.
read.access: Book access varies; course/lab pages public

visual.title: Compiler Explorer
visual.scope: Compile a tiny C function at -O0 and -O2 for explicit ARM64 and x86-64 targets; inspect emitted code, not a playlist.
visual.why: Live source-to-assembly comparison is directly visual and does not introduce a competing assembly curriculum.

units.build: Inspect a C function in Compiler Explorer; compile two translation units with clang and use nm/objdump or readelf to identify symbols and relocations.
units.stop: Stop when one optimization and one relocation can be explained. Do not try to memorize the ISA.

units.title: 8086 decoding and simulation
units.outcome: Decode real 8086 bytes and round-trip course examples, then practice reading compiler-generated x86 disassembly.

read.title: Computer Enhance: 8086 input listings
read.scope: Listings 0037–0057, decoded incrementally: MOV, arithmetic, flags, jumps and memory. Leave later performance listings for phase 4.
read.why: Actual binary/assembly pairs give the decoder a test corpus. Do not copy the reference decoder before writing yours.

visual.title: Computer Enhance: 8086 interlude
visual.scope: Select decoding/simulation lessons corresponding to the listing you are implementing. Subscriber index, not a verified episode deep link.
visual.why: The live instruction-encoding reasoning supports this exact project; do not add a second assembly course.
visual.access: Existing subscription; lesson access not tested

units.build: Decode the selected course listings, reassemble with nasm and compare bytes. Add registers, flags, memory and jumps, then compare final CPU state.
units.stop: Course examples round-trip and CPU state matches. Continue with the existing disassembly labs, not another assembly course.

units.title: Disassembly and stack-boundary labs
units.outcome: Use emitted instructions to recover behavior and inspect the intentionally vulnerable stack boundary.

read.title: CS:APP: Bomb and Attack Lab handouts
read.scope: Only the two lab handouts and intended x86-64 Linux setup. Do not add a general security course.
read.why: These are existing project tests, not duplicate explanations of the ABI lesson.

units.build: Complete Bomb Lab’s six phases and Attack Lab through level 3 using disassembly and the debugger in the isolated lab environment. Draw the recursive stack frame and document how each result follows from instructions.
units.stop: The original lab checks pass and each stack/register transition is explained. Additional exploit research is out of scope.

lookups.title: LLDB / GDB command map
lookups.scope: Only when a debugger command differs between LLDB and GDB.
lookups.why: A reference to unblock inspection, not another study sequence.

lookups.title: ARM A64 Instruction Set guide
lookups.scope: Look up registers, load/store, branches, or a specific instruction encountered in code.
lookups.why: Reference individual instructions rather than memorize a handbook.
lookups.access: Free; URL/edition may redirect by region

excluded.title: Second introductory assembly course on each ISA
excluded.reason: HelloSilicon and Dive Into Systems compare the same small ABI exercises on two targets. Do not add another assembly course or repeat CS:APP chapter 3 after that reading.

excluded.title: A security course alongside the existing labs
excluded.reason: Bomb and Attack Lab remain project exercises. A separate exploit-development curriculum does not help this phase’s required disassembly checks.

4.project: A measured haversine pipeline, SoA hash table and blocked SIMD matmul.
4.core: Correct outputs, repeatable measurements and one explained improvement. Speedup ratios are experiments, not grades.
4.rationale: Algorithmica supplies the bounded written model. Use Computer Enhance demonstrations only for the tool or probe you are building. MIT and conference talks are excluded from the default path because they repeat those outcomes.

units.title: Baseline, timing, and profiling
units.outcome: Measure a correct baseline reproducibly, report inputs/compiler/hardware, and identify the hot stage before changing code.

read.title: Algorithmica: Instrumentation
read.scope: Timing code regions, instrumentation costs and performance counters. Use a monotonic OS clock before attempting raw counters.
read.why: A written measurement method you can implement and test on your Mac.

visual.title: Computer Enhance: profiler demonstrations
visual.scope: Select the initial profiler/repetition-tester material for your haversine stage. The link is the subscriber index, not a guessed episode URL.
visual.why: Watch the tool being built only if the measurement text leaves an implementation gap.
visual.access: Existing subscription; lesson access not tested

units.build: Build the haversine generator/parser baseline, repetition tester and simple block profiler. Record CPU, OS, compiler, flags, data size, checksum, median and minimum.
units.stop: Stop before optimization until output is checked and the measured hot stage is named. Do not time sanitizer builds or include file I/O accidentally.

units.title: Cache hierarchy and memory access
units.outcome: Measure cache/DRAM behavior on native hardware and explain locality and bandwidth with measured data.

read.title: Algorithms for Modern Hardware: Memory Hierarchy
read.scope: Read the Memory Hierarchy chapter; use it only for the cache and memory hierarchy concepts measured in phase probes.
read.why: It is a concise written model to compare against measured Apple Silicon and native x86 results.
read.access: Free online text; chapter navigation is on the linked index

units.build: Write sequential bandwidth and dependent pointer-chase probes; measure cache working sets on the Mac and, only on native x86 hardware, the x86 laptop.
units.stop: Stop with plotted measurements and a stated machine/compiler setup. Do not treat illustrative latency tables as hardware specifications or use emulation for performance claims.

units.title: Branch behavior
units.outcome: Explain predictable and unpredictable branch costs using measured results.

read.title: Algorithms for Modern Hardware: The Cost of Branching
read.scope: The Cost of Branching only. Compare predictable and unpredictable input; inspect whether clang actually emitted a branch.
read.why: The text gives a model for why branch predictability changes performance without adding another full course.
read.access: Free online text; chapter navigation is on the linked index

units.build: Compare sorted and randomized input with branchful and branchless variants. Inspect optimized code, benchmark identical inputs and explain wins or regressions.
units.stop: Stop when the measurement has a plausible bottleneck explanation. Do not adopt branchless code or SoA on style alone.

units.title: Data layout on the same workload
units.outcome: Choose AoS or SoA based on which fields the operation touches.

read.title: Algorithmica: AoS and SoA
read.scope: This one case study. Compare its pointer-chasing workload with your linear scans rather than assuming SoA always wins.
read.why: The contrasting result forces you to reason about access patterns, not style.

units.build: Convert your phase 2 hash table to contiguous metadata/indices. Compare hit and miss probes at a fixed load factor and key distribution. Also compare a scan using all fields with one using a single field.
units.stop: State bytes touched, measured timings and why each layout won or lost on this workload.

units.title: SIMD and the final measured project
units.outcome: Vectorize array addition and the chosen hot loop while preserving a scalar oracle and testing tail lengths.

read.title: Algorithmica: Intrinsics and Vector Types
read.scope: Vector lanes, loads/stores and intrinsic examples. Its code is x86-oriented: translate the lane model to ARM NEON rather than copying AVX on your Mac.
read.why: A bounded written SIMD model; use native-ISA documentation for the exact operations.

visual.title: Computer Enhance: data movement and SIMD
visual.scope: Only the demonstration matching your current cache/SIMD probe. Skip already-understood measurement lessons.
visual.why: Connects the measured bottleneck to emitted loads and instructions on the same project.
visual.access: Existing subscription; lesson access not tested

units.build: First add two arrays with scalar and SIMD versions; test lengths around the lane width. Then optimize the haversine hot loop with NEON on Mac; use AVX2 only on supporting native x86 hardware. Record correctness, error policy, and before/after timings. Finish a scalar matrix multiply, add cache blocking, then SIMD; test irregular dimensions against the scalar oracle.
units.stop: Stop when the scalar oracle agrees within the stated error policy, tails are safe, and results are reproducible. Treat 100x and matmul peak targets as stretch goals, not gates.

lookups.title: Clang loop vectorizer
lookups.scope: Only vectorization diagnostics, aliasing and loop limitations encountered in your own hot loop.
lookups.why: Check whether the compiler vectorized the intended work before replacing it with intrinsics.

lookups.title: Arm NEON intrinsics
lookups.scope: Find the load, add and multiply intrinsic you are actually using; select Neon.
lookups.why: Exact ARM contracts for translating x86-oriented examples.

lookups.title: Dive Into Systems: Cachegrind
lookups.scope: Section 11.5: running Cachegrind and interpreting counts for one existing locality experiment. Use a supported Linux/x86 environment; simulated cache counts are not native Apple performance counters.
lookups.why: An instrument manual, not a second memory-hierarchy explanation.

lookups.title: CMU Cache Lab specification
lookups.scope: Cache Lab self-study writeup: use cache-simulator/transpose checks only as a repair exercise if your existing cache probes do not establish the model. Do not start another performance course.
lookups.why: A written spec with independent checks for a demonstrated cache gap.

excluded.title: Full MIT 6.172 course alongside all Computer Enhance parts
excluded.reason: Duplicates the measurement, cache, branch and SIMD outcomes. Use the selected Algorithmica sections and Computer Enhance demonstrations on one project.

excluded.title: Full Algorithmica HPC curriculum as a parallel track
excluded.reason: Use only its written chapters needed by the current probe; the project and Computer Enhance already cover the sequence.

excluded.title: Acton, Kelley and refterm talk queue
excluded.reason: These are alternate explanations of the measured layout/performance work, not additional assignments after the selected text and demonstrations.

5.project: Selected xv6 labs, a shell, allocator and bounded nonblocking server.
5.core: Match the xv6 course year's book, lab repo and grading scripts. Slow/disconnected clients must not block other clients. The required traps and mmap integration tests also pass; xv6 scheduling work follows the user-space queue in phase 6.
5.rationale: Keep OSTEP as the only conceptual OS text and xv6 as the implementation track. OSTEP chapters are short, public PDFs; assigning Educative's same OS topics or the broad Udemy course would add another pass over processes and paging without replacing the xv6 labs. Narrow the shell, allocator, and network work to one demonstrable mechanism at a time.

units.title: Processes, traps, and system calls
units.outcome: Explain the user/kernel boundary and implement one xv6 system call; make a foreground shell run a command with fork, exec, and wait.

read.title: OSTEP: Process API
read.scope: Read the process creation and control API sections, then stop before scheduling.
read.why: A short primary-text account of fork/exec/wait gives the shell a model; the xv6 lab then shows the kernel side.

visual.title: xv6 book: Traps and system calls
visual.scope: Use the trap/system-call diagrams and the matching xv6 RISC-V book section; do not read the full book in advance.
visual.why: The trap path and register handoff are distinct from OSTEP's API narrative and connect directly to the lab code.

units.build: Run the matching Fall 2025 syscall lab and write a foreground shell for one external command. Once it works, draw descriptor ownership and add redirection plus a two-command pipeline; close unused pipe ends after fork. Then complete the matching traps lab and annotate saved registers and the user/supervisor return boundary; a scheduler experiment follows in phase 6 once the pthread queue is working.
units.stop: The selected xv6 tests pass, the shell reaps children, and pipeline EOF/redirection behave correctly. Full background-job control remains stretch.

units.title: Virtual memory and copy-on-write
units.outcome: Trace virtual-to-physical translation and explain why copy-on-write fork delays copying pages.

read.title: OSTEP: Introduction to Paging
read.scope: Chapter 18: page/frame translation and page-table entries. Use the matching xv6 book figures for Sv39 and COW implementation.
read.why: Adds the concrete paging model missing from a general address-space introduction.

visual.title: xv6 book: Page tables
visual.scope: Use the Sv39 page-table walk and address-space figures alongside the pgtbl/cow lab.
visual.why: The concrete RISC-V address fields and xv6 mappings add architecture-specific visual context rather than repeating the OSTEP abstraction.

units.build: Complete the selected pgtbl and cow exercises; diagram one translation and the page reference/copy path for fork.
units.stop: Stop after the course-year tests pass and the COW explanation matches the code. Do not implement a general-purpose allocator here.

units.title: Filesystems and crash consistency
units.outcome: Follow a file operation through inode, block mapping, and log, and explain what the log protects across a crash.

read.title: OSTEP: File System Implementation (chapter 40)
read.scope: Read the inode, directory, and block mapping discussion; use journaling only to understand xv6's log.
read.why: It supplies vocabulary for the xv6 fs lab without requiring all OSTEP persistence chapters.

visual.title: xv6 book: File system
visual.scope: Follow the filesystem layering and logging figures around the matching book section.
visual.why: The xv6-specific layers and transaction path are useful diagrams not covered by the generic OSTEP chapter.

units.build: Complete the selected xv6 fs exercise and annotate one create/write path from syscall to on-disk blocks.
units.stop: Stop at the selected lab's tests. Do not build a filesystem or read Linux block-layer source as a prerequisite.

units.title: Lazy file mappings and their lifetime
units.outcome: Tie page faults, file references, permissions, unmapping and fork together in xv6.

read.title: xv6 Fall 2025: mmap lab
read.scope: The required mmap/munmap subset and hints only. Skip optional shared-physical-page/unified-buffer-cache challenges.
read.why: This is a new VM/filesystem integration build; it does not repeat the userspace mmap allocator.

units.build: Implement lazy file-backed mmap/munmap, permission checks, MAP_SHARED writeback, and exit/fork reference handling. Run mmaptest and usertests -q; add a protection or reference-lifetime regression test.
units.stop: Both test programs pass and you can trace one fault from VMA lookup to file data and PTE; file references survive descriptor close and are released on unmap/exit.

units.title: A tested userspace allocator
units.outcome: Split and coalesce free blocks without violating alignment or allocation ownership.

read.title: OSTEP: Free-Space Management
read.scope: Chapter 17: tracking free space, splitting, coalescing and placement policies. Skip kernel-specific policy detours.
read.why: This is the allocator mechanism needed by the existing project, not another C memory introduction.

units.build: Build malloc/free over an mmap-backed region in a dedicated test driver. Test alignment, splitting, coalescing, allocation failure and realloc semantics before attempting interposition.
units.stop: The isolated driver passes without lost or overlapping blocks. LD_PRELOAD and replacement of a production allocator remain stretch.

units.title: Bounded nonblocking I/O
units.outcome: Write an echo server that handles partial I/O, a slow reader, and disconnects without blocking other clients.

read.title: Beej's Guide to Network Programming
read.scope: Use the client/server, select/poll, and partial-send discussions; skip unrelated protocol examples.
read.why: A focused sockets reference is more useful here than the broad TLPI volume; the project exercises the actual API contract.

units.build: Implement a level-triggered epoll echo loop with bounded per-client buffers, then test one-byte writes, stalled readers, and mid-message closes. After echo passes, implement the roadmap’s bounded HTTP subset for preloaded fixtures; reject unsupported framing.
units.stop: Slow/disconnected clients do not block others and the documented HTTP subset passes framing/bounds tests. kqueue portability and load targets are follow-ons.

lookups.title: MIT 6.1810 Fall 2025 xv6 course and book
lookups.scope: Use that year's book, lab repository, and scripts as one pinned set.
lookups.why: Lab names and contracts vary by offering; mixing years can make correct work fail tests.

lookups.title: epoll(7)
lookups.scope: Read readiness semantics and level-triggered operation; return for edge triggering only if needed.
lookups.why: The API man page is the contract for the Linux event-loop project.

lookups.title: HTTP/1.1 framing: RFC 9112
lookups.scope: Sections 2, 3 and 6 only while adding the HTTP subset.
lookups.why: A parsing/framing contract, not an additional web course.

lookups.title: CMU Malloc Lab specification
lookups.scope: Malloc Lab writeup and trace-driver conventions only. Choose the existing mmap-backed allocator; the lab memlib scaffold is an alternative harness, not a second allocator assignment. Driver portability to ARM64 is untested.
lookups.why: Adds invariant/test ideas without changing the allocator client or repeating allocation theory.

lookups.title: xv6 Fall 2025: Traps lab
lookups.scope: Backtrace and alarm exercises after the syscall path. Use the same course-year lab repository.
lookups.why: An implementation contract for the trap work, not another OS text.

excluded.title: Educative Operating Systems course lessons on fork and paging
excluded.reason: They overlap the assigned free OSTEP chapters and xv6 book/labs. Keep them as an on-demand alternate explanation only, not parallel required reading.

excluded.title: Fundamentals of Operating Systems (full course)
excluded.reason: A broad second course would duplicate the selected OSTEP and xv6 sequence; no specific distinct lesson is needed for these checkpoints.

6.project: A tested lock-based work-stealing job system and bounded SPSC queue.
6.core: Exactly-once completion, wraparound, shutdown and timeout tests. Lock-free MPMC and weak-memory deques are stretch. Complete the small measured xv6 scheduling experiment after the user-space queue works.
6.rationale: Teach the needed concurrency concepts directly, in C, without making Rust fluency a prerequisite. Bos's freely readable chapters explain atomics and synchronization exceptionally well; use only the sections that support the staged queue/job-system project. CS149 videos add distinct visual explanations of parallel workload behavior, not a second implementation track.

units.title: Threads, races, and publication
units.outcome: Create and join pthreads and distinguish thread-local work from unsynchronized shared state.

read.title: OSTEP: Thread API
read.scope: Chapter 27: create/join and pthread API examples. Skip the already-known process API.
read.why: One short C-based introduction avoids learning Rust syntax before using threads.

units.build: Write a parallel sum with private partial results and join before combining them. Run a separate ThreadSanitizer build; do not benchmark deliberately racy code.
units.stop: Each worker owns its partial result until join, the sum matches a scalar oracle and shutdown cannot leave live threads.

units.title: Mutexes, condition variables, and waiting
units.outcome: Build a bounded mutex/condition-variable queue and state its empty/full and shutdown invariants.

read.title: OSTEP: Condition Variables
read.scope: Chapter 30: predicate loops and producer/consumer example. Do not implement a futex or custom mutex yet.
read.why: A direct pthread-based sleep/wake pattern for the bounded queue.

units.build: Implement a small-capacity pthread queue; test empty waits, full queues, wraparound, and shutdown while workers are idle or have pending work.
units.stop: Stop when timeout-bounded tests complete and each submitted item is handled exactly once. A lock-free MPMC queue is not needed.

units.title: Parallel work and load balance
units.outcome: Measure static chunking, false sharing, and imbalance, and explain why thread count does not translate directly to speedup.

read.title: Rust Atomics and Locks: Understanding the Processor (chapter 7)
read.scope: Read the hardware/cache-coherence sections that explain why writes to shared cache lines contend.
read.why: This is a bounded hardware explanation for the false-sharing measurement, separate from the earlier ordering and lock chapters.

visual.title: Stanford CS149: work distribution (index)
visual.scope: From the pinned schedule, choose only the lecture about work distribution/load balance that matches your static-chunking experiment. Do not watch lectures 1–6 as another queue.
visual.why: The lecture demonstrations add visual execution and workload examples alongside the written cache-coherence explanation.

units.build: Compare adjacent and padded per-thread counters, then parallelize a phase 4 workload with static chunks. Record machine, inputs, and timings. After the user-space scaling tests, instrument the pinned xv6 scheduler for runnable/wait time and try one small policy change. Use kernel locks and timer interrupts already studied in phase 5; compare the behavior on a fixed workload, not a host-thread speed claim.
units.stop: Stop when you can account for the observed scaling and false-sharing result, even if the hardware shows no large speed gap.

units.title: Publication and the bounded SPSC ring
units.outcome: Explain how an acquire observation makes a producer’s preceding writes visible.

read.title: Rust Atomics and Locks: Memory Ordering
read.scope: Chapter 3: relaxed versus release/acquire and happens-before. Read enough of the introduction to understand examples; implement in C11.
read.why: Adds the ordering argument needed to replace the simple single-producer/single-consumer path, not another Rust course.

units.build: First test one-time publication. Then build a bounded SPSC ring with one producer and one consumer; test tiny capacity, wraparound, full/empty transitions and timeout-bounded shutdown.
units.stop: Write the release/acquire and storage-lifetime argument, then pass exactly-once and wraparound stress tests. A clean TSan run is not a proof.

units.title: Locked work stealing
units.outcome: Build a job system with worker-local deques, stealing, wait-helping, and explicit shutdown without guessing weak-memory fences.

read.title: Rust Atomics and Locks: Building Our Own Channels (chapter 5), selected
read.scope: Read the channel ownership and synchronization examples only where they clarify job publication and completion.
read.why: The existing book provides targeted patterns; the phase project intentionally keeps deque synchronization with locks.

units.build: Start with a locked deque per worker and a configurable pool; run exactly-once, uneven-job, waiting-parent, and idle-shutdown tests.
units.stop: Stop when correctness and measured comparison against static chunking are complete. Chase-Lev and lock-free MPMC are stretch work.

lookups.title: ThreadSanitizer documentation
lookups.scope: Use a separate -fsanitize=thread build for executed data-race checks.
lookups.why: A useful detector, but it does not prove deadlock freedom or algorithm correctness.

excluded.title: Full Rust course before concurrency
excluded.reason: The phase uses Rust Atomics and Locks as a concept text and implements in C. Rust syntax is not a prerequisite for pthreads or the C11 memory model.

excluded.title: Full McKenney book and full CS149 course
excluded.reason: Both are substantial references. Select only CS149 lectures for the distinct parallel-performance perspective; consult McKenney only if a concrete coherence question remains.

checks: Speedup plots for every experiment; explain the adjacent/padded counter result even if this hardware shows no dramatic cliff
Ring buffer and queue pass exactly-once, wraparound, shutdown and timeout tests, plus ThreadSanitizer stress with zero reports; record that this is testing, not a correctness proof
Job system runs the matmul within 10% of the hand-split version and handles uneven jobs better
You can explain acquire/release with the diagram above, from memory, and name where your job system needs each
Measure and explain one small xv6 scheduling experiment after the user-space queue works

7.project: Port the hash table and event loop to Rust, with behavior tests and benchmarks.
7.core: Safe containers before unsafe infrastructure. Preserve the C tests and document every unsafe invariant.
7.rationale: The existing phase project is a port of known C behavior, not a demand to finish several Rust courses. Assign small official Rust Book sections at the point of need, then use one bounded linked-list exercise to make ownership constraints concrete. Skip an unsafe arena until the safe port is done.

units.title: Ownership, borrowing, and slices
units.outcome: Port one small tested C container operation using owned values and shared/mutable references without cloning to appease the compiler.

read.title: The Rust Book: Understanding Ownership (chapter 4)
read.scope: Read sections 4.1–4.3, especially references, borrowing, and slices.
read.why: This is the minimum official explanation for moving from manual C ownership to Rust's static rules.

units.build: Port a small hash-table lookup/insert behavior using Vec and slices; retain the C tests as the behavior contract.
units.stop: Stop when tests pass and you can explain each owner and borrow. Do not start an unsafe container to avoid a borrow-checker error.

units.title: Errors at the port boundary
units.outcome: Return failures explicitly and handle them at the program boundary.

read.title: Rust Book: Error Handling
read.scope: Chapter 9, especially recoverable errors with Result and propagation with ?. Review enums/match only if needed to understand these examples.
read.why: A single language mechanism needed by your port’s actual failure paths.

units.build: Port one parser or container API boundary so errors are returned as Result and handled at the CLI/test boundary.
units.stop: Stop when the port preserves the C behavior and makes failure paths visible. Do not add traits or abstractions without a caller that needs them.

units.title: Lifetimes and safe APIs
units.outcome: Explain why a borrowed view cannot outlive its backing allocation and use safe APIs for the hash-table port.

read.title: The Rust Book: Validating References with Lifetimes (chapter 10.3)
read.scope: Read lifetime syntax and the returned-reference example; use lifetimes only when the compiler asks for the relationship.
read.why: A narrow bridge from the phase 2 string-view/arena model to Rust reference validity.

visual.title: Crust of Rust: Lifetime Annotations
visual.scope: Optional worked lifetime example only when a concrete returned-view error blocks the safe port. Do not follow the whole playlist.
visual.why: Watch the compiler constrain the same ownership relationship you have already drawn in C.

units.build: Port the SoA hash table with owned Vec storage and indices where that gives a clearer invariant; benchmark only after equivalent tests pass.
units.stop: Stop with a safe implementation. The optional arena requires a written alignment, stability, aliasing, reset, and destructor contract first.

units.title: Unsafe boundary for the event loop
units.outcome: Keep unsafe code at narrow syscall boundaries and document descriptor, buffer, and lifetime invariants for each block.

read.title: The Rustonomicon: Working with Unsafe
read.scope: Read the unsafe contract and aliasing material relevant to raw pointers and FFI; do not read the whole Nomicon as a prerequisite.
read.why: Unsafe is an explicit contract with callers, not a relaxation of the need to uphold invariants.

units.build: Port the existing event loop and bounded HTTP subset with only the raw libc wrappers they need. Compare behavior tests against the C version; keep descriptor cleanup and buffer ownership visible.
units.stop: The Rust event-loop/server passes the same behavior tests, each unsafe block has a concrete safety comment, and timings are compared with the C version. Async Rust and a full unsafe allocator are out of scope.

lookups.title: Too Many Linked Lists: Learning Ownership
lookups.scope: Use the first ownership-focused chapters as one optional worked example; stop before the book becomes a second full project.
lookups.why: It gives concrete examples of ownership and mutation tradeoffs, but the roadmap's main deliverable remains the C project port.

lookups.title: Bumpalo Bump allocation/reset contract
lookups.scope: Look up allocation and reset semantics only if implementing the optional arena.
lookups.why: Compare a real safe API contract before designing unsafe arena internals.

excluded.title: Read TRPL chapters 1–19 cover to cover plus Rustlings before porting
excluded.reason: That duplicates syntax practice and delays the project's concrete ownership questions. Read selected official chapters as the port needs them; use Rustlings only for a specific syntax gap.

excluded.title: Too Many Linked Lists entire guide and Rust for Rustaceans
excluded.reason: Both are valuable but amount to additional courses. Keep the safe port primary; select a linked-list chapter or advanced reference only to answer a current question.

8.project: Verified reductions and tiled matmul, then optional tensor cores and attention.
8.core: Use the NVIDIA laptop. Compare matched dtype/layout/math modes on your own GPU; no CUDA on macOS.
8.rationale: Use CUDA’s written execution and memory contracts, a tested reduction and Boehm’s first three matmul kernels. Specific GPU MODE profiling/checklist videos add tool context. Do not add PMPP or another full CUDA course; deeper tuning and attention follow the core checkpoint on your NVIDIA laptop.

units.title: Threads, blocks, and indexing
units.outcome: Map output elements to threads and blocks and validate the mapping on irregular dimensions.

read.title: CUDA C++ Programming Guide: Programming Model
read.scope: Read the grid/block/thread model and kernel launch sections needed for vector add and GPU Puzzles.
read.why: The official guide defines CUDA execution semantics and avoids paying for another broad GPU course.

visual.title: GPU Puzzles
visual.scope: Complete the indexing puzzles for elementwise work and reductions; inspect the supplied visual/test feedback.
visual.why: Interactive small tasks make lane and block indexing visible in a way the reference guide does not.

units.build: Run deviceQuery, then write a vector add and test non-multiple sizes against a CPU result.
units.stop: Stop when indexing, bounds, launch errors, and result checks are covered. Skip puzzle repetitions you already solve reliably.

units.title: Memory access and profiling
units.outcome: Measure coalesced versus strided access and use profiler evidence to identify the bottleneck.

read.title: NVIDIA CUDA Best Practices Guide: Memory Optimizations
read.scope: Read global-memory coalescing, shared-memory use, and execution configuration only as they support the probe.
read.why: This section connects the memory model to actionable measurements without assigning the full guide.

visual.title: GPU MODE Lecture 1: How to profile CUDA kernels in PyTorch
visual.scope: Watch for profiler workflow and kernel timing context; timestamps are not specified.
visual.why: A demonstrated profiling workflow adds screen-based tool context distinct from the written memory guide.

units.build: Time a bandwidth probe with CUDA events, compare contiguous and strided access, and inspect one Nsight Compute report.
units.stop: Stop when you can name an observed bottleneck and reproduce the measurement. Do not chase bandwidth numbers from another GPU.

units.title: Reduction before matrix multiplication
units.outcome: Use shared memory and barriers to reduce an irregular input safely.

read.title: CUDA Best Practices: Shared Memory
read.scope: Shared-memory visibility, barriers and bank conflicts only. Start from the programming guide’s kernel model already used in step 1.
read.why: A synchronization contract for the reduction; Boehm’s matmul article is not a reduction tutorial.

units.build: Implement scalar-oracle reduction, then a shared-memory version. Test irregular lengths and block-wide barrier participation with Compute Sanitizer.
units.stop: The reduction matches the stated numerical tolerance and all tested lanes/bounds/barriers are valid.

units.title: Tiled FP32 matrix multiplication
units.outcome: Reuse tiles, measure the bottleneck and handle rectangular/tail shapes.

read.title: Simon Boehm: CUDA Matmul Worklog
read.scope: Implement kernels 1–3 first: naive, coalesced and shared-memory tiling. Later register/warp tiling variants are follow-ons after the core checkpoint.
read.why: Each step changes one data-movement mechanism and records a measurement.

visual.title: GPU MODE: CUDA Performance Checklist
visual.scope: Use only the checklist sections relevant to a bottleneck in your current kernel.
visual.why: A profiler-based diagnostic companion, not a second full CUDA course.

units.build: Implement the tiled kernel with a CPU oracle and irregular M/N/K. Profile it and compare to cuBLAS with matched dtype, layout and math mode; record launch and transfer times separately.
units.stop: Correct reduction and tiled matmul with a stated error policy and an explained profile. Tensor cores, softmax/attention, Triton and Metal are stretch, not an extra prerequisite.

lookups.title: Compute Sanitizer documentation
lookups.scope: Use memcheck and synchronization checks on the kernels under test.
lookups.why: Host sanitizers do not validate device accesses or barriers.

excluded.title: PMPP 4th edition as a full additional textbook track
excluded.reason: Its core topics are already represented by the CUDA guide, GPU Puzzles, targeted GPU MODE lectures, and the Boehm worklog. Use a relevant chapter only to resolve a gap.

excluded.title: Full CUDA Udemy course and GPU MODE playlist
excluded.reason: They add broad setup and repeated memory/kernel coverage. No verified narrow lesson was needed beyond the exact public lectures selected here.

excluded.title: All GPU MODE lectures 3, 4, 8 and 9
excluded.reason: The existing CUDA text, profiler demo, reduction and matmul work already cover these concepts. Keep the scoped lecture-8 checklist, not another viewing queue.

9.project: Build clox in C, then a small protected Lua host.
9.core: clox tests and correct Lua stack/error boundaries first. The required LLVM backend follows in 9b; server hot reload remains stretch.
9.rationale: clox is already the project's compiler/interpreter course and builds a complete bytecode VM with scanner, Pratt parser, compiler, GC, closures, and a VM. Add no C compiler or JavaScript compiler course. Make the Lua comparison a small follow-on: read a few implementation files and prove one host/API path, not the whole Lua runtime.

units.title: Bytecode, chunks, and the VM loop
units.outcome: Trace one expression from source to bytecode and through the stack-based VM.

read.title: Crafting Interpreters: Chunks of Bytecode and A Virtual Machine
read.scope: Read chapters 14–15, covering chunks, the VM, and a test harness. Compiler chapters start in the next unit.
read.why: These exact chapters establish the bytecode representation and dispatch loop without doing the Java tree-walker first.

units.build: Implement the clox chunk/VM sequence and disassemble a small expression; keep the book's tests as behavior checks.
units.stop: Stop when the first expressions execute and you can annotate the stack and instruction pointer. Do not start a second VM project.

units.title: Scanning, Pratt parsing, and compilation
units.outcome: Compile expressions and statements into bytecode while preserving the Lox language behavior contract.

read.title: Crafting Interpreters: Scanning, Parsing Expressions, and Statements
read.scope: Read chapters 16–24 for scanning, Pratt parsing, and the compiler. Skip part 2 unless a chapter refers back to a concept you need.
read.why: This bounded run covers the scanner/parser/compiler needed by clox; no standalone compiler course is necessary.

units.build: Complete the clox scanner and compiler incrementally; test precedence and malformed input as you add syntax.
units.stop: Stop when the required clox compiler tests pass. A C compiler, JavaScript compiler, or native backend is outside this phase.

units.title: Runtime values, garbage collection, and closures
units.outcome: Explain value representation, object lifetime, mark/sweep roots, and captured-variable behavior in clox.

read.title: Crafting Interpreters: Closures
read.scope: Chapters 25–30 in the book’s Part III sequence: closures, GC, classes/methods/inheritance and optimization. Start at Closures, not chapter 15 again.
read.why: Completes the same clox runtime without re-reading the dispatch-loop introduction.

units.build: Finish clox through chapter 30. Force frequent debug collections and test captured locals after their function returns; keep regressions for rooting/lifetime bugs.
units.stop: clox passes the selected book tests and the closure/GC cases. Native code generation and server hot reload are not prerequisites for embedding Lua.

units.title: Lua's VM and the C host boundary
units.outcome: Compare clox's stack VM with Lua's register VM and write a minimal protected Lua call from C.

read.title: The Implementation of Lua 5.0
read.scope: Read the paper's register-VM, table, closure, and coroutine discussion; then inspect only lopcodes.h, lvm.c, and lapi.c in the matching Lua release.
read.why: The short paper gives a visual/conceptual map for selected source files without assigning a full Lua source-reading track.
read.platform: Journal of Universal Computer Science / Lua.org

units.build: Build a tiny C host that loads one script and calls one function via lua_pcall; draw the Lua stack before and after the call.
units.stop: Stop when errors are protected at the C boundary and one clox/Lua instruction comparison is written. Do not read all Lua source or build another compiler.

lookups.title: The Lox Language
lookups.scope: Use as the language behavior contract for the syntax/features actually implemented in clox.
lookups.why: Defines expected behavior without requiring a second tree-walker implementation.

lookups.title: Lua 5.5 Reference Manual
lookups.scope: Use the C API and error-handling sections matching the installed headers/runtime.
lookups.why: The manual, headers, and library version must match at the host boundary.

lookups.title: Lua source releases
lookups.scope: Inspect selected implementation files only, pinned to the same release as the manual.
lookups.why: The versioned source archive is more precise than relying on an unversioned source snapshot.

excluded.title: Developing a C Compiler From Scratch course
excluded.reason: A second compiler project duplicates scanning/parsing/AST concepts while not contributing to the clox or Lua-host deliverables.

excluded.title: Master.dev TypeScript/JavaScript compiler course lessons
excluded.reason: The lessons add a different language and AST formatter track on top of clox. They are not needed to build or understand this C VM.

excluded.title: Crafting Interpreters Java tree-walker part
excluded.reason: The phase specifically chooses the C bytecode VM. Read a tree-walker explanation only when clox refers to a concept that is unclear.

10.project: An SDL3 platform layer, scalar rasterizer, ray tracer and playable build.
10.core: A clipped, depth-tested scalar scene before SIMD or multicore rendering. 1080p60 is stretch.
10.rationale: Build the scalar renderer and SDL3 platform boundary before chasing performance. Handmade Hero is the visual/code walkthrough, but it is C-style C++ on Win32; borrow the data flow and debugging habits, not its OS calls or build setup. The guide exposes topic markers and individual episodes, so select only relevant pages rather than watching days 1–60 in order.

units.title: Pixels, window and platform boundary
units.outcome: Show a moving software-rendered buffer in an SDL3 window; explain pitch, pixel format and ownership.

read.title: SDL3 surface and pixel APIs
read.scope: Surface, pixel formats, pitch and conversion
read.why: The platform contract for presenting a CPU-owned image; do not assume tightly packed rows.

visual.title: Handmade Hero: Allocating a Back Buffer
visual.scope: Episode 3
visual.why: A concrete walkthrough of a CPU backbuffer and its dimensions; translate Win32 presentation to SDL3 rather than copying it.

units.build: Create the SDL3 window and a validated pixel buffer, draw a changing gradient, and present it. Record buffer dimensions, pitch and format.
units.stop: Window input and the gradient work on the target Mac without adding an engine or a separate GPU-renderer curriculum.

units.title: Platform boundary, frame state and replay
units.outcome: Separate OS polling/presentation from update-and-render, measure frame time and replay recorded input.

read.title: Game Programming Patterns: Double Buffer
read.scope: The buffered rendering/state examples only. Keep platform-owned presentation separate from game-owned persistent state; reuse your phase 2 lifetime rules.
read.why: A written explanation of separating an in-progress state from the state being observed.

visual.title: Handmade Hero: Input Recording and Playback
visual.scope: Episode 23
visual.why: A memorable debugging gem: replay makes an intermittent game bug repeatable. Its Win32 file APIs need SDL/platform replacements.

units.build: Use SDL events and performance counters to drive a bounded frame loop. Store input frames and replay a short session to reproduce the same state.
units.stop: Input replay reproduces a state transition and frame timing is logged; defer hot reload and audio until this boundary works.

units.title: Scalar triangle rasterizer
units.outcome: Draw clipped, depth-tested triangles with a documented coordinate, winding and depth convention.

read.title: Scratchapixel: Rasterization, a Practical Implementation
read.scope: Edge functions, barycentric interpolation and perspective-correct interpolation
read.why: Fills the implementation gap from transforms to actual software pixels, with equations tied to diagrams.

units.build: Start with edge-tested 2D triangles, then transform a cube, clip against the near plane before perspective divide, and add a depth buffer. Keep scalar output as oracle.
units.stop: Tests cover shared edges, inside/outside/crossing near-plane triangles, and overlapping depth-tested geometry. SIMD and tiled parallelism are stretch.

units.title: Ray tracing: a separate image-generation mechanism
units.outcome: Trace rays through a camera and simple geometry, then distribute independent pixels safely.

read.title: Ray Tracing in One Weekend
read.scope: Book 1 only. Port the C++ examples to C; the diagrams and rendered images are the visual companion. No books 2–3 yet.
read.why: Ray intersections and sampling are different from rasterization, so the existing project stays in the path.

units.build: Produce book 1’s final image in C, then parallelize tiles using your phase 6 job system. Fix random seeds when comparing output and document sampling limits.
units.stop: The reference scene renders correctly and the parallel version preserves the stated output policy. Extra ray-tracing books are not phase gates.

units.title: A small playable renderer checkpoint
units.outcome: Ship a tiny interactive scene and compare a software image against a minimal GPU presentation path.

read.title: SDL3 application examples
read.scope: Use only a minimal renderer/input example matching your existing window. The goal is packaging a tiny playable build, not learning all sample categories.
read.why: A concrete integration reference for the SDL3 runtime you already use.

units.build: Make a small playable scene with frame-time reporting. If useful, upload the software buffer as a texture for comparison, without replacing the scalar renderer.
units.stop: A second Mac can run the build and the project checklist's scalar correctness is met; 1080p60 is optional.

lookups.title: SDL3 API reference
lookups.scope: Window, events, timing, audio and pixel-format contracts as needed
lookups.why: Primary API reference for the macOS platform layer.

lookups.title: LearnOpenGL: Coordinate Systems
lookups.scope: Return for transform order, clip space and perspective division while building the scalar rasterizer.
lookups.why: A math lookup, not an OpenGL renderer curriculum.

excluded.title: Handmade Hero days 1–60 as a continuous course
excluded.reason: Most are Windows-specific setup and repeated game progression; use exact topic episodes and build on SDL3/macOS instead.

excluded.title: OpenGL/Vulkan renderer as the main project
excluded.reason: The phase's learning target is CPU rasterization. GPU API work belongs to a short comparison or phase 10b.

excluded.title: Ray Tracing books 2 and 3
excluded.reason: Book 1 remains a distinct required project. The later books add depth after that checkpoint.

excluded.title: TinyRenderer as a second rasterizer
excluded.reason: The current scalar renderer and Scratchapixel equations already establish this build. Another renderer would repeat the same deliverable.

11.project: A QEMU kernel with interrupts, paging and two tasks; a separate Pico exercise.
11.core: Boot, faults, mapped memory and cooperative tasks first. Filesystem, user mode and ELF loading are stretch.
11.rationale: Choose the Rust tutorial's boot contract for the QEMU kernel and stay within its Rust/no_std path. Do not mix in the C/assembly bootloader steps from a different tutorial. Keep RP2350 bare metal and Linux modules as independent exercises, not prerequisites for booting the kernel.

units.title: Boot a Rust kernel under its documented loader contract
units.outcome: Build a pinned tutorial-compatible image that boots in QEMU and writes serial output; explain what the bootloader already did.

read.title: Writing an OS in Rust: A Minimal Rust Kernel
read.scope: Second-edition minimal kernel and bootloader contract. Follow the linked freestanding prerequisite once; pin the documented bootimage/bootloader toolchain rather than substituting latest releases.
read.why: The actual boot contract is required reading, not hidden behind an optional companion.

units.build: Follow the tutorial's pinned second-edition bootimage/bootloader contract, add serial output and a panic path, then deliberately trigger a fault in QEMU.
units.stop: Reproducibly boot, print and diagnose one intentional fault. Do not replace the boot protocol as an early exercise.

units.title: Exceptions and hardware interrupts
units.outcome: Install handlers and diagnose intentional exceptions before allowing timer-driven work.

read.title: Writing an OS in Rust: CPU Exceptions
read.scope: Continue in the same tutorial through double faults and hardware interrupts. Diagnose each intentional fault before moving on.
read.why: Keeps exception prerequisites and device interrupts within one known boot path.

units.build: Add breakpoint/double-fault handlers and a minimal hardware timer interrupt. Record which stack/register state the handler owns, and use serial/QEMU diagnostics rather than changing several mechanisms at once.
units.stop: An intentional fault is identifiable and timer interrupts occur without corrupting the interrupted state.

units.title: Page mappings and a usable heap
units.outcome: Distinguish physical frames from virtual pages and keep allocation ownership explicit.

read.title: Writing an OS in Rust: Paging Introduction
read.scope: Follow the same tutorial’s paging, paging implementation and heap-allocation posts. Use its page-table diagrams; no second OSDev boot path.
read.why: This is the missing frame/mapping/heap mechanism between interrupts and tasks.

units.build: Implement frame allocation, map a new virtual region and add a minimal tested heap. Exercise valid mapping, exhausted frames and a deliberate invalid access.
units.stop: Mapping/allocator invariants hold and failures produce a diagnosable panic rather than silent corruption.

units.title: Two cooperative tasks before timer preemption
units.outcome: Switch between two kernel tasks with explicit stack and saved-register ownership.

read.title: MIT xv6 book: Scheduling
read.scope: Scheduling and context-switch discussion, as a conceptual comparison
read.why: A compact reference for process state and switching; do not copy its RISC-V assembly into the x86 Rust tutorial kernel.

units.build: Add cooperative task switching first; only then add a timer interrupt and round-robin policy if the context model is sound.
units.stop: Two tasks resume with their own stack/state and tests show no cross-task memory corruption.

units.title: Separate RP2350 bare-metal exercise
units.outcome: Flash a Pico 2 program that initializes GPIO from the chip documentation and blinks without an SDK runtime.

read.title: RP2350 Datasheet
read.scope: Boot process, selected core/ISA, GPIO and UART chapters
read.why: The datasheet and image format define this board's real boot and register contract; select one core architecture and toolchain.

units.build: First flash a known-good image with documented probe/tools, then write the smallest own startup/GPIO path and a UART message.
units.stop: Known-good recovery route remains available and the chosen board/core path blinks reliably. This is independent of the QEMU kernel.

lookups.title: OSDev Wiki
lookups.scope: Look up an x86 protocol/device detail only when the chosen implementation requires it
lookups.why: Broad reference, not a second boot tutorial to combine with the Rust path.

excluded.reason: Its boot protocol, language and toolchain assumptions differ; mixing them obscures which component owns entry setup.

excluded.reason: The selected tutorial deliberately uses a bootloader and its contract; replacing it is a distinct project.

excluded.reason: xv6 supplies RISC-V experience and the existing Rust kernel has a pinned x86 boot contract. A second boot path would duplicate mechanisms and mix ISA assumptions. Drivers remain separate required work.

12.project: A recoverable single-writer KV store and isolated TCP handshake/echo.

Pin CMU Fall 2025 and select only buffer-pool, index, logging and recovery topics relevant to the B+ tree/WAL; do not enroll in the full course or add the full Udemy course as another prerequisite. Start TCP offline, then use an isolated TUN lab.

units.title: Page format and buffer pool
units.outcome: Serialize a fixed-width page format and manage cached pages with pinning, dirty state and eviction.

14.title: MiniTorch modules 1–4
14.goal: Complete MiniTorch modules 1–4 as a final Python/ML extension, learning autodifferentiation, tensor operations, parallel/GPU kernels, and basic neural-network components while keeping its backend distinct from the native CUDA work.
14.project: Complete and test MiniTorch modules 1–4: scalar autodiff, tensor autodiff, parallel and CUDA tensor operations, then foundational neural-network components.
14.core: Complete modules 1–4 with correctness and numerical gradient checks before training. Module 3 GPU operations require a working NVIDIA CUDA environment from phase 8. MiniTorch uses Python/Numba; it is not a binding to your native CUDA library.
checks: Pass MiniTorch module 1 tests for scalar derivatives and backpropagation, including numerical gradient checks
Pass module 2 tensor indexing, broadcasting, operation, and autodiff tests, including non-contiguous or boundary cases the assignment exposes
Pass module 3 parallel and CUDA operation tests and compare results against the provided/reference backend
Pass module 4 network tests and train the assigned small model with a recorded loss/result
Explain which code runs in MiniTorch's Python/Numba backend and which code belongs to the separate phase-8 native CUDA project
Add an original differentiable operation, test its gradient independently and document the runtime/backend boundary
14.rationale: MiniTorch provides a sequence of public, test-driven modules whose content extends the systems roadmap into autodiff and neural networks. It is a final extension after phase 13, not a substitute for phases 8–9: its CUDA path is Numba-based and is not the native CUDA executable/backend built earlier. Start only after the phase-8 GPU fundamentals and phase-9 VM/compiler work are in place.

units.stop: CPU-parallel and CUDA operation tests both pass on the chosen NVIDIA environment, including reduce and matmul boundary cases. A CPU-only or simulated run is preparation, not completion of the GPU gate.

9b.goal: Add a small numeric LLVM backend after clox, learning explicit IR, verification, JIT execution and object emission without rebuilding an entire language.
9b.project: A numeric expression/function compiler with verified LLVM IR, a JIT path and a linked object-file demo.
9b.core: clox emits bytecode directly, not an AST. Reuse its token and precedence tests, then add a deliberately small C++ AST for numeric expressions/functions. No strings, closures, GC or full Lox lowering. Pin one LLVM version across headers, libraries and tutorial.

Emit and verify LLVM IR for the supported numeric expression/function subset
Run differential tests through clox and the JIT with a documented numeric tolerance
Explain conditional basic blocks, terminators and PHI values
Emit a host-target object, link its caller and add an original feature/test

The C++ tutorial needs a small owning AST because clox has no existing AST to hand to LLVM. Learn unique_ptr at that boundary, not a complete C++ course.

9c.title: CHIP-8 interpreter
9c.goal: Build a small CHIP-8 interpreter as a distinct, tested machine implementation, with instruction behavior, timers, input, and display checked against public ROM tests.
9c.project: Implement a CHIP-8 interpreter with a fetch/decode/execute loop, memory and registers, timers, keypad input, and a pixel display. Keep the build and tests separate from the compiler project.
9c.core: Use Langhoff's implementation guide for the machine model and Timendus ROMs for compatibility checks. Make choices for known CHIP-8 quirks explicit and testable.
checks: Render the CHIP-8 splash and IBM logo ROMs; explain the small opcode subset each checks
Pass the selected Timendus CHIP-8 test ROMs and record any intentionally unsupported quirks
Test instruction decoding, program-counter movement, stack bounds, and memory bounds
Verify timers tick independently of instruction speed and keypad waits resume on a key event
Use a PC/register/opcode debugger with breakpoints and single-step; reproduce one failing instruction trace
9c.rationale: This is a different, concrete interpreter target after the compiler/VM work, not another compiler. Langhoff's guide explains the machine's behavior and historical ambiguities; Timendus supplies practical ROM tests. The interpreter needs its own reproducible build and observable tests rather than relying on a visual demo alone.

units.title: Machine state and instruction cycle
units.outcome: Describe CHIP-8 memory, registers, stack, program counter, timers, and the fetch/decode/execute loop.

read.title: Guide to making a CHIP-8 emulator
read.scope: Read the sections on CHIP-8 architecture, memory, registers, stack, and instruction execution. Note ambiguous or historically variable behavior rather than treating every convention as universal.
read.why: A focused implementation guide for the virtual machine rather than a broad emulator course.

units.build: Define the interpreter state and implement a bounded fetch/decode loop for a small initial opcode set. Add unit tests for instruction effects and program-counter changes.
units.stop: State transitions are tested without a graphical frontend, and invalid memory/program-counter access fails safely.

units.title: Display, keypad, and timing
units.outcome: Connect drawing, input, and delay/sound timers to a runnable CHIP-8 program.

read.title: Guide to making a CHIP-8 emulator
read.scope: Use the guide's graphics, input, and timer sections. Follow its platform-independent machine behavior; choose only the smallest local display/input layer needed to run ROMs.

visual.title: Timendus: expected IBM logo in Octo
visual.scope: Run the reference ROM to see its expected frame; compare with your own emulator. This demo does not prove keypad or timer correctness.
visual.why: A runnable expected-output view, not a second emulator tutorial.

units.stop: Logo frames match; dedicated keypad tests pass and timers remain 60 Hz when opcode throughput changes. The splash screen alone does not check input.

units.title: Compatibility tests and deliberate quirks
units.outcome: Use public ROM tests to find opcode errors and document selected compatibility behavior.

read.title: Timendus CHIP-8 test suite
read.scope: README usage and the CHIP-8 test ROMs relevant to the implemented instruction set. Do not claim support for SUPER-CHIP or XO-CHIP unless implemented and tested.
read.why: The ROMs check real interpreter behavior and expose commonly missed display, arithmetic, and quirk differences.

units.build: Run the relevant ROMs; for each failure, reduce it to an instruction-level regression test. Choose and document behavior for shift, index-register, and sprite edge cases based on the intended compatibility target.
units.stop: The selected CHIP-8 ROM tests pass or each remaining incompatibility is named and explained. Do not imply extensions are supported by base CHIP-8 tests.

units.title: Single-step debugger and an ownership extension
units.outcome: Explain a failing opcode by inspecting machine state instead of guessing from the display.

read.title: Langhoff: instructions and quirks
read.scope: Consult only the failing opcode or selected quirk; no rereading the whole implementation guide.
read.why: The spec is the debugger contract; there is no reference implementation to copy.

units.build: Add PC/register/opcode view, breakpoint and single-step controls; capture one reduced failure. Then add save/load state or a bounded instruction trace with a round-trip/regression test. Record the tested ROM revision and a clean build command.
units.stop: You can stop before a bad instruction, state the violated invariant, and replay or restore the same state. No Game Boy/NES or extension-ISA detour.

excluded.reason: The task is a tested base CHIP-8 interpreter. Extension support adds distinct opcodes and display rules and should not be claimed without separate implementation and tests.

excluded.reason: The learning target is a small interpreter with a visible machine loop; a larger framework would obscure that deliverable.

11b.goal: Build and test a character device, an observed interrupt/deferred-work path and a controlled mapping in the lab’s QEMU x86 guest, with explicit kernel and architecture assumptions.
11b.project: A character device with a bounded read/write interface, an interrupt-driven event path with deferred work, and a deliberately small mmap demonstration.
11b.core: First validate the supplied QEMU x86 setup on the existing x86 laptop, recording uname -m, target kernel and pinned lab revision. Load modules only into that matching guest. On Apple Silicon, x86 requires explicit emulation/cross-building, not an ARM64 guest pretending to be the same target; no host kernel modules.
checks: Build and load a minimal module against the exact target VM kernel, then unload it cleanly
Exercise character-device read/write behavior from a user process and test bounds and error paths
Trace interrupt top-half versus deferred work without sleeping in interrupt context
Map and unmap the documented buffer and explain its lifetime and permissions
Unload safely while deferred work is pending and record the observed IRQ source
11b.rationale: This is a required, bounded Linux driver extension, not a second kernel. Use the existing x86 laptop as the lab host and boot the lab’s QEMU x86 target; verify its bitness instead of assuming x86-64. Pin the lab tree, VM/kernel and matching docs together. Native Apple Silicon ARM64 virtualization does not run x86 instructions.

units.title: Validate the QEMU lab target first

read.title: Linux Kernel Labs: Booting the virtual machine
read.scope: Only Booting the virtual machine and the provided QEMU/GDB workflow. Pin the lab revision and match its kernel/build scripts; skip source-navigation tools and unrelated disk exercises.
