units.build: Boot the provided lab target on the existing x86 laptop; record lab commit, QEMU command, uname -m, kernel release and module build tree. Build/load/unload the minimal supplied module in the guest only. Do not assume the public master docs match an arbitrary modern distribution kernel.
units.stop: The target and build architectures are stated, modules load only into their matching kernel, and the lab's supported test path passes.

units.title: Character device and user/kernel boundary
units.outcome: Register a small character device and define its read/write contract, ownership, and error behavior.

read.title: Linux Kernel Labs: Character device drivers
read.scope: The character-device lab only: module setup, registration, file operations, and the user-space test program.
read.why: It gives a concrete driver/user boundary and lab scaffold without requiring a second kernel implementation.
read.access: Public course material; VM and lab setup requirements are in the lab instructions

units.build: In the compatible lab VM, complete the character-device exercise, then add one bounded read/write behavior and test short buffers, invalid requests, and cleanup.
units.stop: The module builds against the running VM kernel, user-space tests pass, and unload leaves no registered device behind.

units.title: Device access and observed interrupts
units.outcome: Acknowledge the lab device event and state which handler operations cannot sleep.

read.title: Linux Kernel Labs: I/O access and Interrupts
read.scope: I/O ports versus MMIO, device acknowledgement and interrupt-handler exercise only. The next step handles deferred execution separately.
read.why: The lab supplies an actual device/IRQ exercise; deferred execution is the next step, not a second explanation here.
read.access: Public course material; hardware-dependent parts may require the lab's supported setup

units.build: Run the supplied x86/QEMU I/O and IRQ exercise on its documented device. Record event generation, handler invocation and acknowledgement, then repeat events and test cleanup. If the current VM lacks that device, repair the matching lab setup before moving on; do not replace evidence with a conceptual diagram.
units.stop: The supported lab device produces an observed interrupt, acknowledgement is correct and the handler cannot sleep. Record the device and VM path; conceptual reading alone does not pass this build.

units.title: Deferred work and safe shutdown
units.outcome: Move slower work out of interrupt context and close the race between queued work and module removal.

read.title: Linux Kernel Labs: Deferred work
read.scope: Workqueue exercise and cancellation/cleanup rules. Compare softirq/tasklet context only to explain where sleeping is forbidden; do not implement every deferred-work mechanism.
read.why: A distinct execution/lifetime contract following the IRQ lab.

units.build: Queue bounded work from the observed event path, record top-half and worker context, then stress shutdown/unload with work pending. Flush/cancel work before freeing module state.
units.stop: Deferred work executes in its documented context and repeated load/event/unload tests leave no queued work or use-after-free.

units.title: Map a kernel buffer to a process
units.outcome: Use mmap for one controlled buffer and state who may access it and how long it remains valid.

read.title: Linux Kernel Labs: Memory mapping
read.scope: The memory-mapping lab sections that implement a device mapping and test it from user space; skip unrelated memory-management topics.
read.why: It supplies a direct mapping example and makes the user/kernel lifetime and access contract visible.
read.access: Public course material; follow its stated kernel and VM requirements

units.build: Complete the mapping lab's small example. Add a user-space test for mapped contents and cleanup, and document mapping permissions and buffer lifetime. Do not turn this into a DMA or zero-copy claim.
units.stop: Mapping and unmapping follow the documented lab contract, and tests demonstrate allowed access and cleanup.

lookups.title: Linux Kernel Labs: Interrupts lecture
lookups.scope: Linux interrupt handling and interrupt context, only when interpreting the interrupt lab.
lookups.why: A course lecture reference for interrupt context and deferred execution.

11c.title: Embedded firmware
11c.goal: Extend the existing RP2350 bare-metal exercise by understanding the Cortex-M core, interrupts, GPIO, timers, serial I/O, and DMA constraints without turning it into another kernel project.
11c.project: A register-aware timer/UART/ring-buffer firmware with an event loop in the RP2040 simulator; document the port boundary to the existing RP2350 board exercise.
11c.core: Use one RP2040 C-compatible firmware core in Wokwi: register-level GPIO, timer/UART interrupts, a bounded ring and a cooperative event loop. SDK startup/interrupt registration is allowed, but explain the reset/vector path and inspect the generated code. Wokwi models one CPU core and DMA only for PIO; no dual-core or general DMA evidence is implied. Hardware is not required.
checks: Trace RP2040 reset/vector/interrupt entry and compare the existing RP2350 ARM boot path
Run register-aware GPIO and timer interrupts in the selected C/C++ Wokwi scaffold
Test UART ISR-to-main-loop ring wraparound, overflow and partial input
Run a cooperative event/state-machine loop with bounded ISR work
Document target register differences and DMA lifetime rules without claiming unsupported simulation
11c.rationale: Deepen the existing Pico exercise, not another kernel. The hardware-free route uses Wokwi RP2040 Cortex-M0+ with an SDK C/C++ scaffold; it is not RP2350 Cortex-M33. Arm’s second-edition Nucleo-F091RC text supplies concepts, while the RP2040 datasheet defines registers. Keep the original RP2350 startup exercise separate and make a port map, not another complete firmware implementation.

units.title: Cortex-M core, exceptions, and interrupt state
units.outcome: Trace exception entry, vector selection, and the state saved by the selected Cortex-M core.

read.title: Arm Education: Embedded Systems Fundamentals, chapters 3 and 4
read.scope: Second-edition Nucleo-F091RC book: chapter 4 core/interrupt entry, with chapter 3 only for ISR/main-loop coordination. Skip general thread/race explanations already covered in phase 6; do not copy STM32 register addresses.
read.why: The official page publishes the chapter contents and links a free textbook; these chapters address concurrency, core state, and interrupts without adding another architecture course.
read.access: Free PDF via official Arm Education repository; board examples differ from RP2040/RP2350.

units.build: Start from the Wokwi Pico C++ SDK scaffold and keep the firmware logic C-compatible. Locate reset/vector/stack setup in the built image, trigger a timer interrupt and inspect the handler path. Use the RP2040 datasheet, not the textbook’s STM32 addresses.
units.stop: You can trace reset to main and vector to handler for RP2040, and distinguish this scaffold from the owned RP2350 boot exercise.

units.title: GPIO and timer-driven behavior in simulation
units.outcome: Configure a pin and replace busy waiting with a timer-driven event in one supported simulator target.

read.title: Arm Education: Embedded Systems Fundamentals, chapters 2 and 7
read.scope: Chapter 2, General Purpose Input/Output, and chapter 7, Timers, for the concepts and exercises. Examples target a different STM32 board; use the RP2040 datasheet and Wokwi target for actual registers and peripherals.
read.why: The public contents confirm these focused topics, while the separate RP2040 reference keeps simulator-specific work grounded in the actual target.
read.platform: Arm University; Raspberry Pi documentation for target details
read.access: Free PDF via official Arm Education repository; board examples differ from RP2040/RP2350.

visual.why: A visible simulator target with a concrete compiled firmware scaffold.
visual.access: Public browser example; local/VS Code features may have separate access requirements.

units.build: Drive one GPIO using the RP2040 register contract, then switch from a busy loop to a timer interrupt. Inspect generated assembly for the MMIO accesses; keep ISR work to acknowledgement and posting a bounded event.
units.stop: The GPIO changes at the configured timer cadence and the handler stays bounded; document the single simulated CPU and target registers.

units.title: Serial diagnostics and peripheral data flow
units.outcome: Use UART output to observe a peripheral event and reason about buffering and concurrency.

read.title: Arm Education: Embedded Systems Fundamentals, chapters 8 and 3
read.scope: Chapter 8: UART framing and buffering only. Reuse the ISR/main-loop coordination model from step 1 rather than reread chapter 3. Verify target-specific UART registers against the RP2040 datasheet.
read.why: The chapter list confirms serial and concurrency coverage. The target datasheet, not the textbook example, defines the Pico peripheral contract.
read.platform: Arm University; Raspberry Pi documentation for target details
read.access: Free PDF via official Arm Education repository; board examples differ from RP2040/RP2350.

units.build: Use the physical UART interface wired to the serial monitor, not USB Serial disguised as UART. Move RX bytes from the ISR through a bounded ring into the main loop; handle overflow explicitly and test wraparound, partial messages and a slow consumer. Add a cooperative state-machine task that consumes events without sleeping in the ISR.
units.stop: UART traffic and timer events coexist; ring overflow/wraparound tests pass and the main loop, not the ISR, handles slower work.

units.title: DMA and the RP2350 hardware boundary
units.outcome: Read the RP2350 DMA contract and identify which properties cannot be established by the selected simulator.

read.title: RP2350 Datasheet
read.scope: Compare only the GPIO, UART, timer, selected ARM core and boot assumptions needed to port this RP2040 exercise. Read DMA transfer lifetime/buffer rules conceptually; do not assume the simulator models arbitrary DMA.
read.why: This is the chip's primary hardware contract. Wokwi's Pi Pico project targets RP2040 and does not establish RP2350 or DMA behavior.

units.build: Write an RP2040-to-RP2350 port map against the two datasheets without rebuilding both implementations. Design one DMA transfer with buffer lifetime and completion/interrupt rules. General DMA is a written model unless real supported hardware is available; Wokwi’s documented DMA support is PIO-only.
units.stop: The port map names changed core/startup/register assumptions, and the DMA design states what was modeled versus measured. No hardware purchase or fabricated simulator result is required.

lookups.why: Wokwi's Pico simulator is RP2040, so use the matching chip reference rather than the RP2350 datasheet.

lookups.title: Wokwi Pico model and UART wiring
lookups.scope: Supported peripherals, physical UART serial-monitor wiring and model limitations. DMA is PIO-only; only one core is simulated.
lookups.why: The simulator feature table bounds what tests can establish.
